title: Devilled Kidneys on Toast
subtitle: Lamb's kidneys in a spiced butter and Worcestershire sauce on hot toast
excerpt: Devilled kidneys are a British breakfast and brunch classic from the Victorian and Edwardian eras: halved lamb's kidneys cooked fast in a devilling sauce of butter, Worcestershire sauce, mustard, and cayenne, served on buttered toast. The sauce is sharp, hot, and savoury; the kidneys must be barely cooked through.
sourceNotes: Devilled kidneys were a standard dish of the Victorian and Edwardian grand breakfast table, appearing in cookbooks of the period alongside devilled chicken and devilled bones. The term 'devilling' refers to the high-heat cooking method with spiced, mustard-heavy sauces.

content.text: Devilled kidneys take about 8 minutes from start to plate. Like calves' liver, lamb's kidneys must cook fast: medium-high heat, 2 to 3 minutes per side, and out. Overcooked kidneys turn grainy and develop a strong ammonia note. The devilling sauce is assertive by design: cayenne, mustard, and Worcestershire all pushing in the same direction.

items.prepNote: halved, membrane and core cut out

attrs.title: Preparing the kidneys
attrs.body: Cut each kidney in half and use scissors or a small knife to remove the white core and surrounding membrane. This core is what causes the stronger flavour , once removed, the kidney is mild and sweet.

content.text: Mix together the Worcestershire sauce, English mustard, and cayenne in a small bowl. Set aside.

Heat {{unsalted-butter}} of butter in a frying pan over medium-high heat until foaming. Season the kidney halves with salt and add them cut-side down. Cook for 2 to 3 minutes without moving until browned. Turn and cook for 2 minutes more. They should be just faintly pink in the thickest part.

Pour the devilling sauce into the pan and bubble for 30 seconds, tossing the kidneys to coat. Add a squeeze of lemon juice. Tip onto buttered toast and scatter over the chopped parsley. Serve immediately.

items.symptom: The kidneys have a strong, unpleasant smell
items.cause: The white core and membrane were not fully removed.
items.fix: Remove the entire white core with scissors. It is the main source of the strong flavour that can make kidneys off-putting. Once trimmed, the kidney should smell mild and faintly sweet.

items.symptom: The kidneys are tough and grey all the way through
items.fix: Kidneys overcook very fast. 2 to 3 minutes per side over medium-high heat is the maximum. A slightly pink centre is correct.

items.symptom: The sauce has evaporated by the time the kidneys are done
items.cause: The pan was too hot and the sauce reduced to nothing.
items.fix: Add the devilling sauce only in the last 30 seconds. Its job is to coat, not to braise.

items.symptom: The dish lacks heat and bite
items.cause: The cayenne or mustard was reduced.
items.fix: This is a devilled dish , it should be clearly spiced. Increase the cayenne to 0.5 teaspoon and use English mustard, not Dijon.

content.text: Devilled kidneys belonged to the Victorian breakfast table alongside smoked haddock and kedgeree. They fell out of fashion as offal became less common on British menus, but they never entirely disappeared. The combination of hot, savoury, and buttery on toast is a very British idea of comfort, and the technique is fast enough for a weekday brunch when you have good kidneys to hand.
